title: A practical primer on FLIM and FRET‐FLIM for quantitative bioimaging
authors: Görkem S. Ulkar; Dinesh Beniwal; Maddy Parsons; Simon M. Ameer‐Beg
matched_keywords: biosensor; bioimaging; fluorescence lifetime imaging; flim
abstract: Abstract Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) measures the fluorescence decay time of a fluorophore and can therefore provide information that is not available from fluorescence intensity alone. Changes in lifetime can report on the local molecular environment and, through Förster resonance energy transfer measured by FLIM (FRET‐FLIM), on interactions occurring over nanometre length scales. In this primer, we describe the basic principles of FLIM and FRET‐FLIM and introduce two widely used time‐domain acquisition approaches: time‐correlated single‐photon counting and time‐gated detection. We then consider practical aspects of planning a FLIM experiment, including fluorophore choice, photon statistics, instrument response, sample preparation, and the challenges associated with imaging live and three‐dimensional specimens. Three applications are used to illustrate how lifetime measurements can be applied in biological experiments: label‐free metabolic imaging using NAD(P)H and FAD, intramolecular FRET biosensors that report conformational or signalling changes, and intermolecular FRET‐FLIM for studying protein–protein interactions. We also discuss commonly used analysis approaches, available software, and routes through which researchers can access FLIM instrumentation. The final section considers current efforts to improve measurement standardisation and analysis, together with the growing use of computational methods and the combination of FLIM with other microscopy modalities.

title: Fluorescence lifetime imaging of NAD(P)H and flavin: A practical introduction to studying metabolic heterogeneity in living samples
abstract: Abstract Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) of cellular autofluorescence allows metabolism to be visualised in living systems without exogenous labelling. By measuring the decay characteristics of NADH, NADPH and flavin autofluorescence, FLIM can be used to investigate metabolic heterogeneity within intact cells, tissues and developing organisms while preserving spatial and temporal context. Despite increasing adoption, newcomers to the field often encounter difficulties in experimental design, data analysis and metabolic interpretation. This primer therefore aims to provide a practical introduction to the principles and implementation of autofluorescence FLIM. The photophysics of NAD(P)H and flavins are summarised and the instrumental requirements for FLIM are introduced. Key aspects of experimental design are considered and approaches to fluorescence decay analysis are reviewed. The metabolic insights that can be obtained from the fitted parameters are discussed alongside the limitations of interpreting fluorescence lifetimes as direct measures of pathway activity. These concepts are illustrated through a case study in which NAD(P)H FLIM was used to identify a previously unrecognised metabolic gradient during the development of hearing. The primer advances the view that, while a sensitive reporter of metabolic state, autofluorescence FLIM alone is best viewed as a powerful hypothesis‐generating tool. When combined with targeted perturbations and orthogonal validation approaches, it provides a uniquely informative means of characterising metabolism within complex living systems.
